```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
library(BayesianQDM)
```

## Decisions in a proof-of-concept study

BayesianQDM implements the Bayesian quantitative decision-making framework
of Kang, Yamaguchi and Han (2026) for proof-of-concept (PoC) studies. The
data of a PoC study lead to one of three decisions: Go (proceed to the next
phase of development), NoGo (stop the development) or Gray (the evidence is
not sufficient for either decision).

Let $\theta$ be the treatment effect, the difference between the treatment
and control groups in the response rate (binary endpoint), the mean
(continuous endpoint) or the survival probability at a milestone time
(time-to-event endpoint), or the ratio of the hazards of the two groups
(time-to-event endpoint). The decision criteria use two values of the effect
chosen by the study team: the target value $\theta_{TV}$, an effect worth
pursuing, and the minimum acceptable value $\theta_{MAV} < \theta_{TV}$,
below which the treatment is not of interest. Given the PoC data $D$, the
criteria based on the posterior probability are

- Go criterion: $\Pr(\theta > \theta_{TV} \mid D) \ge \gamma_{go}$,
- NoGo criterion: $\Pr(\theta \le \theta_{MAV} \mid D) \ge \gamma_{nogo}$.

The decision is Go if only the Go criterion is met, NoGo if only the NoGo
criterion is met, and Gray if neither is met. If both are met, which for one
endpoint is possible only when $\gamma_{go} + \gamma_{nogo} \le 1$, the
decision is called Miss; the package reports Miss decisions separately and
warns when they have positive probability.

Kang et al. (2026) write the NoGo criterion as
$\Pr(\theta > \theta_{MAV} \mid D) \le \gamma_2$. This is the same criterion
with $\gamma_{nogo} = 1 - \gamma_2$, so a threshold $\gamma_2 = 0.2$ of the
article corresponds to `gamma_nogo = 0.8`.

When smaller effects are favorable, as for the rate of an adverse event or
a hazard ratio, `direction = "less"` in the criterion reverses the
inequalities: the Go criterion is
$\Pr(\theta < \theta_{TV} \mid D) \ge \gamma_{go}$ and the NoGo criterion
is $\Pr(\theta \ge \theta_{MAV} \mid D) \ge \gamma_{nogo}$, with
$\theta_{TV} < \theta_{MAV}$ (see `vignette("single-binary")` and
`vignette("time-to-event")`).

The criteria can instead be based on the posterior predictive probability of
the effect $\tilde\theta$ that will be observed in a future study with $m_t$
and $m_c$ subjects. With a null value $\theta_{NULL}$, the Go criterion is
$\Pr(\tilde\theta > \theta_{NULL} \mid D) \ge \gamma_{go}$ and the NoGo
criterion is $\Pr(\tilde\theta \le \theta_{NULL} \mid D) \ge \gamma_{nogo}$.

For two endpoints, the target values and minimum acceptable values divide
the plane of $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ into nine regions, and the criteria are
based on the probabilities of unions of regions or on each endpoint
separately (see `vignette("two-binary")` and `vignette("two-continuous")`).

## Specifying a study

A study is described by small specification objects, which are combined into
a design.

| Function | Specifies |
|---|---|
| `prior_beta()`, `prior_nix()`, `prior_dirichlet()`, `prior_niw()`, `prior_gamma()`, `prior_vague()` | Prior distribution of one group |
| `data_binary()`, `data_continuous()`, `data_binary2()`, `data_continuous2()`, `data_tte()` | Summary of the data of one group |
| `borrow()` | External data and the weight $a_0$ of the power prior |
| `hypothetical()` | Hypothetical control for a study without a concurrent control group |
| `criterion_posterior()`, `criterion_predictive()` | Decision criterion |
| `conduct_tte()` | Enrollment, dropout and time of the analysis of a study with a time-to-event endpoint |
| `design_binary()`, `design_continuous()`, `design_binary2()`, `design_continuous2()`, `design_tte()` | Design of the study |
| `qdm_endpoint()` and the steps that follow it | Design of the study, built step by step (see below) |

The control group of a design takes one of four forms: a concurrent control
group (`n_c` of at least 1 for binary and time-to-event endpoints, 2 for one
continuous endpoint and 3 for two continuous endpoints), external control
data only (`n_c = 0` and `external_c`), a hypothetical control (`n_c = 0`
and `hypothetical_c`), or a fixed control (`n_c = 0` and `fixed_c`), a known
value of the control parameter as in a single-arm study compared with a
benchmark.
External data can also be borrowed for the treatment group (`external_t`).

Six functions work with the designs.

| Function | Computes |
|---|---|
| `qdm_decide()` | The probabilities of the Go and NoGo regions and the decision for observed data |
| `qdm_oc()` | The operating characteristics: the probabilities of Go, NoGo, Gray and Miss decisions under scenarios for the true parameters |
| `qdm_compare()` | The operating characteristics of several designs under the same scenarios, in one table |
| `qdm_calibrate()` | The thresholds $\gamma_{go}$ and $\gamma_{nogo}$ that control the probabilities of a false Go and a false NoGo decision |
| `qdm_find_n()` | The smallest candidate sample size for which the probabilities of meeting the Go and NoGo criteria under two scenarios are at most given targets |
| `qdm_boundary()` | The observed data that lead to each decision, for example the numbers of responders, with the observed rates and effects (not available for two binary endpoints) |

## A first example

Consider a PoC study with one binary endpoint, 12 subjects in each group and
Jeffreys priors $\textrm{Beta}(0.5, 0.5)$. The team chooses
$\theta_{TV} = 0.2$, $\theta_{MAV} = 0.1$, $\gamma_{go} = 0.5$ and
$\gamma_{nogo} = 0.8$.

```{r design}
des <- design_binary(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12,
  prior_t = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5), prior_c = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5),
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = 0.2, theta_mav = 0.1,
                                  gamma_go = 0.5, gamma_nogo = 0.8)
)
des
```

If 9 of 12 subjects respond in the treatment group and 4 of 12 in the control
group, the decision is:

```{r decide}
dec <- qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_binary(12, 9),
                  data_c = data_binary(12, 4))
dec
```

The posterior probability that the effect exceeds the target value is
`r format(dec$prob_go, digits = 3)`, and the decision is
`r dec$decision`.

The operating characteristics show how often the design leads to each
decision. For a binary endpoint all outcomes of the study are enumerated, so
the probabilities are exact.

```{r oc, fig.alt = "Probabilities of the decisions against the true difference in response rates"}
oc <- qdm_oc(des, data.frame(pi_t = seq(0.3, 0.7, by = 0.05), pi_c = 0.3))
oc
plot(oc)
```

When the treatment has no effect ($\pi_t = \pi_c = 0.3$), the probability of
a Go decision is `r format(oc$Go[1], digits = 3)`. The thresholds can be
calibrated so that the probability of meeting the Go criterion is at most
0.05 under no effect, and the probability of meeting the NoGo criterion is at
most 0.2 when the effect is 0.3:

```{r calibrate, fig.alt = "Probabilities of meeting the Go and NoGo criteria against the threshold, with the targets and the chosen thresholds"}
cal <- qdm_calibrate(des,
                     scenario_go = data.frame(pi_t = 0.3, pi_c = 0.3),
                     scenario_nogo = data.frame(pi_t = 0.6, pi_c = 0.3),
                     target_go = 0.05, target_nogo = 0.2)
cal
plot(cal)
```

The calibrated thresholds are $\gamma_{go} =$ `r cal$gamma_go` and
$\gamma_{nogo} =$ `r cal$gamma_nogo`, and `cal$design` is the design with
these thresholds, which can be passed to `qdm_decide()` and `qdm_oc()`.
In the plot, the dashed horizontal lines are the targets and the dotted
vertical lines are the chosen thresholds, in the colors of the criteria.

`qdm_boundary()` shows which observed data lead to each decision. For each
number of control responders, it gives the numbers of treatment responders
that lead to Go, NoGo and Gray decisions, the corresponding observed
response rates of the treatment group and the observed differences in
response rates:

```{r boundary, fig.alt = "Regions of the decisions by the numbers of control and treatment responders"}
b <- qdm_boundary(des)
b
plot(b)
```

The numbers written on the regions are the boundary values, such as the
smallest number of treatment responders that leads to a Go decision. With
4 control responders, a Go decision needs at least
`r min(b$from[b$y_c == 4 & b$decision == "Go"])` of the 12 treatment
subjects to respond.

## Building a design step by step

A design can also be built step by step, for example with the native pipe
`|>` of R. `qdm_endpoint()` starts a specification for an endpoint, and
each of the other steps sets some arguments of the `design_*()` function of
the endpoint:

| Step | Arguments |
|---|---|
| `qdm_sample_size()` | `n_t`, `n_c` |
| `qdm_prior()` | `prior_t`, `prior_c` |
| `qdm_criterion()` | `criterion` |
| `qdm_external()` | `external_t`, `external_c` |
| `qdm_control()` | `hypothetical_c`, `fixed_c` |
| `qdm_tte()` | `milestone`, `effect`, `conduct`, `conduct_future` (time-to-event endpoint) |
| `qdm_computation()` | `method`, `nMC`, `enumerate` |

```{r pipe}
spec <- qdm_endpoint("binary") |>
  qdm_sample_size(n_t = 12, n_c = 12) |>
  qdm_prior(prior_t = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5),
            prior_c = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5)) |>
  qdm_criterion(criterion_posterior(theta_tv = 0.2, theta_mav = 0.1,
                                    gamma_go = 0.5, gamma_nogo = 0.8))
spec
```

`qdm_build()` creates the design by calling `design_binary()` with these
arguments, so it is the design `des` of the first example:

```{r pipe-build}
identical(qdm_build(spec), des)
```

The steps only store their arguments, which are checked when the design is
built, so the error messages are those of the `design_*()` function. A
design created by a `design_*()` function can also start a pipe, and the
steps then change parts of it. A step sets all its arguments anew, both when
it is given again and when it is applied to a design (an argument that is
not given returns to its default). The analyses
(`qdm_decide()`, `qdm_oc()`, `qdm_compare()`, `qdm_calibrate()`,
`qdm_find_n()` and `qdm_boundary()`) accept a specification and build it,
so the pipe can go on to the analysis, here the operating characteristics
with 20 subjects in each group:

```{r pipe-oc}
spec |>
  qdm_sample_size(n_t = 20, n_c = 20) |>
  qdm_oc(data.frame(pi_t = seq(0.3, 0.7, by = 0.1), pi_c = 0.3))
```

`vignette("pipe")` gives more examples with the pipe, including
`show_report()`, which writes the design and its results as a draft of the
corresponding sections of a study protocol.

## Plots

The `plot()` methods return ggplot2 objects. Depending on the plot, their
arguments set the colors of the decisions (`col_go`, `col_nogo`, `col_gray`
and `col_miss`), the width of the lines (`linewidth`), the size of the points
(`point_size`), the size of the text drawn in the plot (`label_size`), the
base font size (`base_size`) and the position of the legend
(`legend_position`); the help pages of `plot.qdm_oc()`,
`plot.qdm_calibration()`, `plot.qdm_boundary()`, `plot.qdm_decision()`,
`plot.qdm_comparison()` and `plot.qdm_n_search()` list them. Anything else
can be changed by adding ggplot2 functions, as for any other ggplot2 plot:

```{r plot-style, fig.alt = "Operating characteristics drawn with other colors, line width, font size, legend position and a title"}
plot(oc, col_go = "darkgreen", col_nogo = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.7,
     base_size = 13, legend_position = "right") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Operating characteristics of the design")
```

The plot of a decision shows how the observed data lead to it, here with
the posterior density of the treatment effect and the Go and NoGo regions:

```{r plot-decision, fig.alt = "Posterior density of the difference in response rates with the Go and NoGo regions"}
plot(qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_binary(12, 9),
                data_c = data_binary(12, 4)))
```

## Endpoints and computation

| Endpoints | Design | Model | Probabilities of the regions | Operating characteristics |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One binary | `design_binary()` | Beta-binomial | Numerical integration (posterior), exact sum (predictive) | Exact enumeration |
| One continuous | `design_continuous()` | Normal-Inverse-chi-squared or vague | Numerical integration (`"NI"`), moment matching (`"MM"`) or Monte Carlo (`"MC"`) | Simulation of `nsim` studies |
| Two binary | `design_binary2()` | Dirichlet-multinomial | Monte Carlo with `nMC` draws (posterior), exact sum (predictive) | Exact enumeration or simulation |
| Two continuous | `design_continuous2()` | Normal-Inverse-Wishart or vague | Moment matching (`"MM"`) or Monte Carlo (`"MC"`) | Simulation of `nsim` studies |
| One time-to-event | `design_tte()` | Exponential with Gamma prior (milestone survival or hazard ratio) | Numerical integration or F distribution (posterior), simulation of `nMC` future studies (predictive) | Simulation of `nsim` studies |

The posterior distributions have closed forms, including those with external
data borrowed through a power prior, so Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling is
not needed. With a fixed control, the probabilities depend only on the
posterior distribution of the treatment group and are computed from closed
forms or by numerical integration, except for the posterior probabilities of
two binary endpoints and the predictive probabilities of a time-to-event
endpoint, which are Monte Carlo estimates. For one continuous endpoint, numerical integration is exact up
to a small numerical error; the moment-matching approximation is faster by
about two orders of magnitude for operating characteristics and is suited
to exploring designs, and the
chosen design can then be checked with numerical integration. For two
continuous endpoints, the moment-matching approximation can be checked with
Monte Carlo estimates. The computing time of
Monte Carlo estimates is proportional to the number of draws, and that of
simulated operating characteristics to `nsim`.

## Random numbers

`qdm_decide()`, `qdm_oc()`, `qdm_compare()`, `qdm_calibrate()`,
`qdm_find_n()` and `qdm_boundary()` have a `seed` argument for
the random numbers they use (simulated studies and Monte Carlo estimates of
probabilities). With `seed = NULL` (the default) they use the current random
number stream, so `set.seed()` makes the results reproducible. With a given
seed, the computation uses that seed and the previous state of the random
number generator is restored on exit. `ptdiff()` with `method = "MC"` and
`rdirichlet()` always use the current random number stream.

When the operating characteristics are simulated, the thresholds chosen by
`qdm_calibrate()` and the sample size chosen by `qdm_find_n()` can change
with the simulation error if the probabilities are close to the targets, so
a larger `nsim` (and `nMC`) than for exploring designs is advisable for the
final design.

## Validation

The scripts in the folder `validation` of the installed package compare
BayesianQDM with published and submitted results (Kang et al., 2026; Huang,
Talukder, Han and Kuan, 2019; Huang et al., submitted; Yamaguchi, Homma,
Takeda and Maruo, submitted; Yamaguchi et al., submitted). The file
`results/summary.md` in that folder reports the comparisons, with a
registered reason for every difference beyond rounding:

```{r validation, eval = FALSE}
system.file("validation", "results", "summary.md", package = "BayesianQDM")
```
